growth_story.headline: Tuvalu's income per person stalled from 1999 to 2012, then rose on fishing fees and externally financed building to a new high in 2025, in big swings.
growth_story.arc: Since 1990, Tuvalu's income per person has grown in three eras: 4.6 percent a year in 1990–1998, -0.5 in 1999–2012 and 3.6 in 2013–2025. The sources say little about what drove the 1990s. For the middle era, the IMF in 2014 described weak, volatile growth and remittances from seafarers that had not recovered since the global financial crisis. The turn came as fishing license fees more than doubled under a regional scheme that sells fishing days, and externally financed building followed, from housing for regional summits to coastal defences. Growth averaged 3.2 percent a year over 2016–2025, up from 1.6 over 2006–2015, and income per person reached a new high in 2025, but the path swung hard: up 15.3 percent in 2019 and down 9.1 in 2022, the last year of the pandemic closure. The sources now describe an economy carried by grants, fishing fees and public works, with more people leaving.

threads.title: Fishing fees transform the budget
threads.text: From the early 2010s, a regional scheme that sells days of tuna fishing, plus joint ventures with Asian fishing firms, more than doubled what Tuvalu earned from fishing licenses. By 2017 the IMF counted fishing revenue as a far larger share of the economy than in 2011. This new money arrived as the faster 2013–2025 era began.

growth_story.tension: The data put income per person above its 2019 level by 2024 and at a new high in 2025. But the IMF, writing in 2025, says the economy as a whole has not recovered: "real GDP has not yet reached its pre-pandemic level". Income per person also grew faster in 2023 and 2024 (5.4 and 5.2 percent) than the total growth the sources report. Both gaps fit a shrinking population, which matches the rising emigration the IMF describes, but no source reconciles the two measures.
